text: Unit 7, 7.1. So, Hamed, shall we continue working on our group presentation? Good idea, Yoriko. Now, Daniel and Samia are focusing on the environmental issues of fast fashion. So, we'll be talking about copyright infringement. Daniel said they've already written their part of the presentation, you know. Wow, really? We've only just got started on ours. Anyway, we're focusing on the way that fast fashion companies lift unknown artists' designs and put them onto their products, which they then sell in huge numbers. That's right. So, first, I think we should talk about what happened to Vanessa Bowman. The artist from the south of England who paints the world around her? Yes, views out onto her garden, natural scenes, that sort of thing. A fast fashion company lifted images of her paintings they found on her website and used them on a clothing range. I'm sure they made a lot of money and I don't think she got anything in return. No, she didn't get anything. No payment, no credit for her work, nothing. She's not alone, though. No, we should also use the example of Kirstie Moran. She creates interesting, unusual designs of animals. Her artwork was also used by a fast fashion company and again, she got nothing from them. I mean, this is a perfect example of a company taking an artist's designs without permission and using them to sell clothes and make a profit. What can anyone do? Some large fashion companies take legal action when their designs are copied, but it takes money and power to do that. It's just not practical for an independent artist like Kirstie Moran to say, if you don't pay me for my hard work and talent, I'll be contacting my lawyer. Well, I have seen some examples of artists defending their intellectual property, but not many. Alora Petra, for example. I haven't read about her yet. She did do something about it after she discovered that a fast fashion company was converting her designs into images and putting them on clothing and bags. At first, Alora decided it wasn't worth complaining to them by email, so she tried a different approach. She posted her complaint on social media and it went viral. Thousands of people from all over the world criticized the company and promised never to buy anything from them again. Finally, the company wrote to her offering an apology. They actually paid her something for using her work and promised it would never happen again. That's one happy ending, at least. Not quite. The same companies lifted her work several times since then and used it on all sorts of products. Although they've accepted it was their fault again, she still hasn't received a second payment. She's going to be disappointed this time, I imagine. The thing is, these companies do have the ability and the resources to collaborate with artists, pay them for their designs, and still make a lot of money, but they choose not to. I know. It's plagiarism, basically, and it's not ethical. Oh, I do agree. Imagine doing that sort of thing at our university. Can you see the situation changing anytime soon? No, I don't think it will change. In a few years, these companies will be ignoring copyright law just like they do now, and artists still won't be getting anything.
